Large data and GPUs

Source: vignettes/articles/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd

A survey of a few hundred plots trains in seconds on a laptop with the default settings. An archive of a million plots takes the settings this article covers: the learning rate and its schedule, the batch size, the size of the model, the encoding settings that bound memory, and the GPU settings, from mixed precision to what happens when the GPU runs out of memory.

Each section says what a setting does in the RESOLVE engine. The examples run on the small survey that ships with the R package, so they show the calls and what they return; the speed and memory effects only appear on large data. The GPU settings need the CUDA build of the RESOLVE engine and are shown without being run.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/resolve/r")

# The RESOLVE engine library, downloaded once
library(resolveR)
resolve.install_backend()
pip install resolve-core

Installing the RESOLVE engine covers the GPU build.

The survey

The survey has 150 plots in the Alps, each with its elevation and habitat, and the species recorded on each plot with its genus, family and cover. The roles name the columns of the two tables, and each target is a column to impute.

plots <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "plots.csv", package = "resolveR"))
species <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "species.csv", package = "resolveR"))

roles <- list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
              abundance = "cover", genus = "genus", family = "family")
targets <- list(
  elevation = list(column = "elevation", task = "regression"),
  habitat = list(column = "habitat", task = "classification")
)
dataset <- resolve.dataset.frame(plots, species, roles = roles,
                                 targets = targets)
import pandas as pd
import resolve_core as rc

data = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gcol33/resolve/master/r/inst/extdata/"
plots = pd.read_csv(data + "plots.csv")
species = pd.read_csv(data + "species.csv")

roles = rc.RoleMapping()
roles.plot_id = "plot_id"
roles.species_id = "species"
roles.abundance = "cover"
roles.genus = "genus"
roles.family = "family"

targets = [rc.TargetSpec.regression("elevation"),
           rc.TargetSpec.classification("habitat", 4)]
dataset = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets)

Training and reading the fit introduces the training settings and how to pass them.

Learning rate

The learning rate scales each step the optimizer, AdamW, takes. Its default is 0.001, with a weight decay of 0.0001; both are training settings.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, lr = 1e-3, maxEpochs = 100L,
                             trainConfig = list(weight_decay = 1e-4),
                             verbose = FALSE)
fit$trainer$get_config()[c("lr", "weight_decay")]
#> $lr
#> [1] 0.001
#> 
#> $weight_decay
#> [1] 1e-04
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.lr = 1e-3
cfg.weight_decay = 1e-4
cfg.max_epochs = 100
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
trainer.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
result = trainer.fit()
round(trainer.config.lr, 6), round(trainer.config.weight_decay, 6)
#> (0.001, 0.0001)

The default is a reasonable start for the hash, embed, sparse and rank-pool encodings. Attention layers react more strongly to the rate: with the transformer encoding and at least one attention layer, a lower rate such as 0.0003 is a common start.

The loss curve tells you which way to move it:

  • The loss jumps or turns to NaN within a few epochs: lower the rate by a factor of 3 to 10.
  • The loss falls slowly and levels off high: raise it by a factor of 3 to 10.
  • The loss swings up and down without a downward trend: lower it by a factor of 2 to 3.

Schedules

A schedule changes the rate during the run. By default none runs and the rate stays at lr. Four schedules are available:

  • step multiplies the rate by lr_gamma (default 0.1) every lr_step_size epochs (default 100).
  • cosine lowers the rate along a cosine from lr to lr_min (default 0.000001), reached at the last epoch of max_epochs.
  • linear lowers the rate at every optimizer step to lr_min at the end of max_epochs.
  • plateau follows the held-out fold and lowers the rate when the held-out value stops improving.
step <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, maxEpochs = 100L, fixedEpochs = 100L,
                              verbose = FALSE,
                              lrScheduler = "step", lrStepSize = 30L,
                              lrGamma = 0.1)
signif(step$result$lr[c(1, 30, 31, 61, 91)], 3)
#> [1] 1e-03 1e-03 1e-04 1e-05 1e-06

cosine <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, maxEpochs = 100L, fixedEpochs = 100L,
                                verbose = FALSE,
                                lrScheduler = "cosine", lrMin = 1e-6)
signif(cosine$result$lr[c(1, 25, 50, 75, 100)], 3)
#> [1] 0.001000 0.000862 0.000508 0.000150 0.000001
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 100
cfg.fixed_epochs = 100
cfg.lr_scheduler = rc.LRSchedulerType.StepLR
cfg.lr_step_size = 30
cfg.lr_gamma = 0.1
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
step = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
step.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
step_rates = step.fit().lr_history
[float(f"{step_rates[epoch - 1]:.3g}") for epoch in [1, 30, 31, 61, 91]]
#> [0.001, 0.001, 0.0001, 1e-05, 1e-06]

cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 100
cfg.fixed_epochs = 100
cfg.lr_scheduler = rc.LRSchedulerType.CosineAnnealing
cfg.lr_min = 1e-6
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
cosine = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
cosine.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
cosine_rates = cosine.fit().lr_history
[float(f"{cosine_rates[epoch - 1]:.3g}") for epoch in [1, 25, 50, 75, 100]]
#> [0.001, 0.000862, 0.000508, 0.00015, 1e-06]

Both runs train a fixed 100 epochs, so the rate history, the rate each epoch trained at, covers the whole schedule. The step schedule drops the rate after every 30 epochs; the cosine schedule ends at lr_min on the last epoch. Both are laid out over max_epochs, so a run that early stopping ends sooner never reaches their end. The plateau schedule and a linear warmup at the start of the run are covered in Training and reading the fit.

Batch size

The batch size is the number of plots per optimizer step. A smaller batch takes more steps per epoch with noisier gradients, which acts as a regularizer on a small dataset; a larger batch keeps a GPU busy. The default is 4096, larger than the whole survey, so each epoch here is one step.

small_batch <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, batchSize = 32L,
                                     maxEpochs = 100L, verbose = FALSE)
small_batch$result$effective_batch_size
#> [1] 32
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.batch_size = 32
cfg.max_epochs = 100
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
small_batch = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
small_batch.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
small_batch.fit().effective_batch_size
#> 32

Starting points to try, and to measure on your own data:

Plots Batch size
under 10,000 512 to 2048
10,000 to 100,000 4096
over 100,000 8192 to 16384

When you raise the batch size, the learning rate usually has to rise with it. Memory grows linearly with the batch size under every encoding. The transformer encoding also holds an attention matrix whose size grows with the square of the number of species per plot, so there the cap on species per plot matters as much as the batch size (Pool weighting and capping).

Model size

hidden_dims sets the depth and the width of the shared encoder, by default six layers of 2048, 1024, 512, 256, 128 and 64 units. The last width is the width of the latent representation, the vector each plot is encoded into.

small <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, hiddenDims = c(256L, 128L, 64L),
                               maxEpochs = 100L, verbose = FALSE,
                               modelConfig = list(dropout = 0.3,
                                                  head_dropout = 0,
                                                  use_residual = TRUE))
sapply(small$trainer$compute_diagnostics()$layers, `[[`, "n_neurons")
#> [1] 256 128  64
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.hidden_dims = [256, 128, 64]
model_config.dropout = 0.3
model_config.head_dropout = 0.0
model_config.use_residual = True
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 100
model_config = rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset, model_config)
small = rc.Trainer(rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, model_config), cfg)
small.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
small_result = small.fit()
[layer.n_neurons for layer in small.compute_diagnostics().layers]
#> [256, 128, 64]
  • Small datasets (under 5,000 plots): the deep default can overfit before it converges; three layers of 256, 128 and 64 units are a better start.
  • Mid-size datasets: 512, 256 and 128 units, or the default.
  • Large datasets: the default, made wider if the training loss levels off above the held-out loss.
  • With the transformer encoding: the attention layers already carry capacity, so a shallower stack above them is usually enough.

dropout (default 0.3) applies between the encoder’s layers and head_dropout (default 0) inside the heads, one per target. use_residual adds residual connections between the encoder’s layers, which helps a deeper stack train.

Early stopping

Early stopping watches the loss on the held-out fold and ends the run when it has not improved for patience epochs (default 50), within the limit of max_epochs (default 500). The weights of the best epoch are restored, so a larger patience never returns a worse model, it only costs epochs. Starting points:

Use Patience
Quick experiments 10 to 20
Standard training 30 to 50
Final runs 100
Attention layers, which converge more slowly 50 to 100

An epoch counts against the patience only once the loss has reached the phase it will be in at the last epoch; Training and reading the fit explains the phases.

Encoding settings

The encoding settings are dataset settings, passed when the data is loaded (Encoding the species set). Three of them decide how much memory the species take.

Hash width

The hash encoding maps each species to one of hash_dim buckets (default 32). More buckets mean fewer species share one, and a wider input layer. 64 and 128 are the usual next steps on a large species list. The selection decides which species reach the hash at all: the default keeps the three most abundant species of each plot (selection = "top", top_k = 3); "all" keeps every species.

hashed <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "hash", hash_dim = 64L, selection = "all")
)
dim(hashed$hash_embedding())
#> [1] 150  64
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Hash
data_config.hash_dim = 64
data_config.selection = rc.SelectionMode.All
hashed = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                       config=data_config)
tuple(hashed.hash_embedding.shape)
#> (150, 64)

The model takes the hash width from the dataset (in Python through rc.model_config_for_dataset()), so it needs no setting of its own. Measure the effect of a wider hash on your own data.

Pool weighting and capping

The rank-pool and transformer encodings read every species of a plot, padded to a common width. pool_weighting sets the weight each species carries in the pooling; the default, log1p, compresses the range of the abundances while keeping their order, so the dominant species weigh most without the rest being ignored. The other weightings are binary, abundance, norm and rank.

pool_species_cap bounds the padded width, the largest term in the memory these encodings use:

  • 0 (default): no cap; the plot with the most species sets the width.
  • A negative value: a percentile cap, read as 100 minus the value: -1 caps at the 99th percentile of species per plot, -5 at the 95th.
  • A positive value: a fixed cap.

A plot longer than the cap keeps its most abundant species, so the kept set does not depend on the order of its records. Here a cap of 4 cuts the survey’s plots, which hold up to 8 species, to their 4 most abundant.

uncapped <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "rank_pool")
)
capped <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "rank_pool", pool_weighting = "log1p",
                pool_species_cap = 4L)
)
c(uncapped = ncol(uncapped$pool_weights()), capped = ncol(capped$pool_weights()))
#> uncapped   capped 
#>        8        4
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.RankPool
uncapped = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                         config=data_config)
data_config.pool_weighting = rc.PoolWeighting.Log1p
data_config.pool_species_cap = 4
capped = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                       config=data_config)
{"uncapped": uncapped.pool_weights.shape[1], "capped": capped.pool_weights.shape[1]}
#> {'uncapped': 8, 'capped': 4}

A cap drops species, so it changes what the model sees. Leave it at 0 for a result you publish unless the uncapped run does not fit in memory, and report the cap if it does not.

Transformer settings

The transformer encoding has its own model settings: the width of each species token (d_model), the attention heads (n_heads), the attention layers (n_attention_layers), the width of the feed-forward layer inside each block (transformer_ff_dim, normally 2 to 4 times d_model) and how the tokens are pooled into one vector per plot (transformer_pooling). Pooling with cls reads a separate token that sees the species only through attention, so it needs at least one attention layer.

tokens <- resolve.dataset.frame(plots, species, roles = roles,
                                targets = targets,
                                config = list(species_encoding = "transformer"))
attn <- resolve.train.dataset(tokens, dModel = 64L, nHeads = 4L,
                              nAttentionLayers = 2L, transformerFfDim = 128L,
                              transformerPooling = "attention", lr = 3e-4,
                              maxEpochs = 50L, verbose = FALSE)
attn$result$best_epoch >= 0
#> [1] TRUE
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Transformer
tokens = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                       config=data_config)
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.d_model = 64
model_config.n_heads = 4
model_config.n_attention_layers = 2
model_config.transformer_ff_dim = 128
model_config.transformer_pooling = rc.TransformerPooling.Attention
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.lr = 3e-4
cfg.max_epochs = 50
model_config = rc.model_config_for_dataset(tokens, model_config)
attn = rc.Trainer(rc.ResolveModel(tokens.schema, model_config), cfg)
attn.prepare_data(tokens, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
attn.fit().best_epoch >= 0
#> True

GPU settings

Training on a GPU needs the CUDA build of the RESOLVE engine: resolve.install_backend(variant = "cuda") in R, and the CUDA wheel in Python (Installing the RESOLVE engine). The code in this section is shown without being run, since this site is built on a machine without a GPU.

Device and mixed precision

The device is a training setting: "cuda" for the current GPU, "cuda:N" for GPU number N. A missing CUDA device is an error.

Mixed precision (AMP, automatic mixed precision) runs most operations in 16-bit floating point and keeps the sums that need the range in 32 bits. It is off by default. Its loss scaling starts at amp_init_scale (default 65536), grows by amp_growth_factor (2) after amp_growth_interval (2000) steps without overflow and shrinks by amp_backoff_factor (0.5) after one.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(
  dataset, device = "cuda",
  trainConfig = list(use_amp = TRUE, amp_init_scale = 65536,
                     amp_growth_factor = 2, amp_backoff_factor = 0.5,
                     amp_growth_interval = 2000L)
)
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.device = "cuda"
cfg.use_amp = True
cfg.amp_init_scale = 65536.0
cfg.amp_growth_factor = 2.0
cfg.amp_backoff_factor = 0.5
cfg.amp_growth_interval = 2000
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
trainer.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
result = trainer.fit()

The normalization layers run in 32 bits inside the mixed-precision region, so batch-normalization statistics cannot overflow the 16-bit range. If the loss turns to NaN a few steps into a mixed-precision run with attention layers, turn mixed precision off before changing anything else.

cuDNN and TF32

Two settings trade exact reproducibility for speed on the GPU. cudnn_benchmark (default true) lets cuDNN, NVIDIA’s library of network primitives, time several algorithms on the first batches and keep the fastest for inputs of a fixed shape. allow_tf32 (default true) runs 32-bit matrix products in the TF32 format on Ampere and later GPUs. Both are applied once when the run starts and hold for the whole run.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(
  dataset, device = "cuda",
  trainConfig = list(cudnn_benchmark = FALSE, allow_tf32 = FALSE)
)
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.device = "cuda"
cfg.cudnn_benchmark = False
cfg.allow_tf32 = False

Data on the GPU

On a GPU, the trainer copies the training and held-out folds to the device once and takes each batch there, so no batch crosses from main memory during the epochs. This has no setting.

With the hash encoding, the dataset setting use_cuda_hash computes each batch’s hash on the GPU instead of when the data is loaded. The trainer then computes the next batch’s hash on a separate CUDA stream while the current batch runs through the model, so the two overlap. This also has no setting of its own.

hashed <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "hash", use_cuda_hash = TRUE)
)
fit <- resolve.train.dataset(hashed, device = "cuda")
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Hash
data_config.use_cuda_hash = True
hashed = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                       config=data_config)
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.device = "cuda"
model = rc.ResolveModel(hashed.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(hashed))
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
trainer.prepare_data(hashed, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
result = trainer.fit()

Limiting GPU memory

PyTorch keeps the GPU memory it has used in a cache for reuse. vram_fraction caps that cache at a share of the GPU’s memory. The default, 1, sets no cap, so a training job alone on a GPU uses all of it. Set a lower value when the GPU also drives a desktop: on Windows, the graphics driver moves allocations beyond the GPU’s memory into main memory, which can freeze the desktop under load. The cap only limits memory; a desktop that turns slow without freezing is short of GPU compute, which it does not address.

The same cap applies when a saved model is loaded onto a GPU, and it can be set on its own, before any model is built.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, device = "cuda",
                             trainConfig = list(vram_fraction = 0.8))
predictor <- resolve.load("model.pt", device = "cuda", vram_fraction = 0.8)

resolve.set_vram_fraction(0.8)
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.device = "cuda"
cfg.vram_fraction = 0.8
predictor = rc.Predictor.load("model.pt", device="cuda", vram_fraction=0.8)

rc.set_vram_fraction(0.8)

On a machine without a GPU, setting the cap does nothing. The command line takes --vram-fraction for resolve train and resolve predict (The command line).

Allocator configuration

PyTorch reads the settings of its GPU memory cache from the environment variable PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF when it first allocates on a GPU. Importing resolve_core sets it to the RESOLVE engine’s default, unless it is already set; in R, resolve_configure_cuda_allocator() sets it. The default depends on the platform:

Platform Setting
Linux, macOS expandable_segments:True,garbage_collection_threshold:0.8,max_split_size_mb:256
Windows garbage_collection_threshold:0.8,max_split_size_mb:256

expandable_segments lets the cache grow and release its memory in place, which keeps it from fragmenting; PyTorch does not support it on Windows, so the RESOLVE engine leaves it out there. garbage_collection_threshold:0.8 makes the cache free unused blocks when it holds more than 80 % of its cap, and max_split_size_mb:256 keeps it from splitting large free blocks into small pieces. On Windows these two reduce fragmentation less than expandable_segments does on Linux, so a job close to the memory cap there may need a smaller batch.

The function returns the setting in effect; force overwrites a value set elsewhere. It acts only when it runs before the first GPU allocation of the process, so in R call it before the first training run on a GPU.

resolve_configure_cuda_allocator()
resolve_configure_cuda_allocator(force = TRUE)
rc.default_cuda_alloc_conf()
rc.configure_cuda_allocator()
rc.configure_cuda_allocator(force=True)

Running out of GPU memory

When the GPU runs out of memory during training, the trainer frees the optimizer state, the mixed-precision state and the cached memory, halves the batch size and starts the run again from the first epoch with the starting weights. It halves at most down to batch_size_floor (default 1024); when halving would go below it, the original out-of-memory error is raised with the batch size asked for, the size reached and the floor. The effective batch size in the result is the size the run trained at; the checkpoint records it as the run’s batch size, with the floor.

fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, device = "cuda", batchSize = 16384L,
                             trainConfig = list(batch_size_floor = 1024L))
fit$result$effective_batch_size
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.device = "cuda"
cfg.batch_size = 16384
cfg.batch_size_floor = 1024
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, cfg)
trainer.prepare_data(dataset, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
trainer.fit().effective_batch_size

The self-supervised pretraining runs the same retry, down to its own batch_size_floor, and caps the cache at its own vram_fraction (Latent and species embeddings). On Linux the allocator setting delays running out of memory; on Windows the halving recovers when fragmentation leaves no other way. On the command line: resolve train --batch-size 16384 --batch-size-floor 1024.

Starting points

The three recipes below are places to start from, to be adjusted against the loss curve and the held-out metrics.

A quick experiment: the hash encoding over every species, a small encoder and a short run.

quick_data <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "hash", hash_dim = 64L, selection = "all")
)
quick <- resolve.train.dataset(quick_data, hiddenDims = c(256L, 128L, 64L),
                               maxEpochs = 50L, patience = 10L,
                               batchSize = 4096L, verbose = FALSE)
round(quick$result$final_metrics$habitat$accuracy, 3)
#> [1] 0.9
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.Hash
data_config.hash_dim = 64
data_config.selection = rc.SelectionMode.All
quick_data = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                           config=data_config)
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.hidden_dims = [256, 128, 64]
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 50
cfg.patience = 10
cfg.batch_size = 4096
model_config = rc.model_config_for_dataset(quick_data, model_config)
quick = rc.Trainer(rc.ResolveModel(quick_data.schema, model_config), cfg)
quick.prepare_data(quick_data, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
round(quick.fit().final_metrics["habitat"]["accuracy"], 3)
#> 0.8

Standard training: a mid-size encoder and a longer run.

standard <- resolve.train.dataset(quick_data, hiddenDims = c(512L, 256L, 128L),
                                  maxEpochs = 200L, patience = 30L,
                                  batchSize = 4096L, verbose = FALSE)
round(standard$result$final_metrics$habitat$accuracy, 3)
#> [1] 0.8
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.hidden_dims = [512, 256, 128]
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 200
cfg.patience = 30
cfg.batch_size = 4096
model_config = rc.model_config_for_dataset(quick_data, model_config)
standard = rc.Trainer(rc.ResolveModel(quick_data.schema, model_config), cfg)
standard.prepare_data(quick_data, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
round(standard.fit().final_metrics["habitat"]["accuracy"], 3)
#> 0.833

A longer run with the rank-pool encoding on a GPU: log-weighted pooling, cover dropout (cover_dropout, which during training replaces the cover values of a random share of the plots in each batch with presence alone), a patient early stop and mixed precision.

pooled_data <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species, roles = roles, targets = targets,
  config = list(species_encoding = "rank_pool", pool_weighting = "log1p")
)
pooled <- resolve.train.dataset(pooled_data, coverDropout = 0.1,
                                maxEpochs = 300L, patience = 100L,
                                device = "cuda",
                                trainConfig = list(use_amp = TRUE))
data_config = rc.DatasetConfig()
data_config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.RankPool
data_config.pool_weighting = rc.PoolWeighting.Log1p
pooled_data = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets,
                                            config=data_config)
model_config = rc.ModelConfig()
model_config.cover_dropout = 0.1
cfg = rc.TrainConfig()
cfg.max_epochs = 300
cfg.patience = 100
cfg.device = "cuda"
cfg.use_amp = True
model_config = rc.model_config_for_dataset(pooled_data, model_config)
pooled = rc.Trainer(rc.ResolveModel(pooled_data.schema, model_config), cfg)
pooled.prepare_data(pooled_data, test_size=0.2, seed=42)
result = pooled.fit()
